projects.title: LangChain GTM Agent: an in-house sales agent that builds deal documents
projects.what: The agent LangChain uses every day for its sales team: call prep, outreach drafts and above all sales artifacts (account plans, proof-of-value docs, proposal decks, onboarding plans). Think of it as a junior SDR/sales ops hire living in Slack. Harrison Chase's retweet is truncated; details come from LangChain's November 10 post about this agent.
projects.how: Built on the Deep Agents harness (the frame that runs the model with its tools). A rep asks for a document in Slack, or the agent offers one during meeting prep. It reads the account in Salesforce plus call transcripts and product usage data, asks the rep for missing inputs, copies the leadership-approved template from Google Drive, and builds the document in a sandbox (an isolated machine with python-pptx, LibreOffice and the brand kit). It then reviews itself: converts to PDF, turns pages into images, checks them, fixes and re-renders. Finally it files a native Google Slides/Docs/Sheets file and posts a PDF preview and link in Slack, flagging what a human should check. Sales process rules live in skills versioned apart from the code, and every run is traced in LangSmith.
projects.who: A concrete case of agents doing real business work. Reported results over 12 weeks: 1,540 artifacts generated (100+ per week), 47% of deals that received an artifact moved to a later stage versus 16% without, and 337 hours of rep time saved on sent artifacts. A stopping rule (ship as soon as a review finds no real defect) cut a one-pager from 18 to 7 minutes.
projects.try: The agent itself is not open source; LangChain publishes a GTM agent template (Salesforce, Gmail, Slack, BigQuery) and points to Deep Agents / Managed Deep Agents to build the equivalent.

projects.title: Warp Learn: a free course to build your own software factory
projects.what: A hands-on course from Warp that starts with a backlog agent (the agent that handles the to-do list of tickets) and builds up to a multi-stage factory with specs, verification and risk assessment. Zach Lloyd also shares Ben Holmes's guide, which he calls the most comprehensive he has seen.
projects.how: According to the course description, a factory is made of agents (who do the work), automations (what triggers them: a new ticket, a Slack message), runners (the machines they run on), skills, scorers (what grades the work) and benchmarks (reference tasks to compare configurations). You start with a triage agent that labels tickets as ready to build, needs more info or duplicate, then add stages and human approval gates at the risky points. Ben Holmes's guide covers encoding factory steps as code, where to put human gates, and what verification and risk assessment look like.
projects.who: The right starting point to go from vibe coding with one agent to agents working through a queue of tasks on their own. The triage, execution, verification, human approval logic also applies to non-technical ops.
projects.try: Free, 3 units. The warp.dev site could not be reached, so details come from the tweet and course descriptions found in search.

projects.title: Claude artifacts become installable desktop apps
projects.what: Ask Claude to build an artifact (a mini web app), click Install as app, and it opens like any other app on Mac or Windows. In plain terms: an internal tool built without coding that lives in your dock.
projects.how: The app can use your connectors (Claude's links to Gmail, Drive, Slack and so on), OS APIs and Claude itself, and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item.
projects.who: For ops people, the shortest path to small internal tools (a deal tracker that notifies you, a reporting widget) without deploying anything. Relayed by @dexhorthy (skeptical) and @kieranklaassen (enthusiastic).
projects.try: Available now in the Claude app on Mac and Windows. The announcement link could not be read, so details are limited to the tweet.

projects.title: Agent Approve 0.9: approve your agents' actions from your watch
projects.what: An app that tracks what your agents do and asks your permission for sensitive actions from an iPhone or Apple Watch. Version 0.9 adds Policy Rules powered by Jev, TypeSafe AI's judgment model, plus an Ask List.
projects.how: Instead of approving everything by hand, Jev checks each agent action against your rules: safe actions go through automatically, doubtful ones are sent to you. Human-in-the-loop approval, but sorted automatically.
projects.who: Trust is the main blocker for agents at work. This kind of tool lets an agent run without constant supervision. Relayed by @CompleteSkeptic, who also highlights another Jev use: report, Jev classifier, grouping, new issues sent to Slack.
projects.try: Solo and Pro plans, prices not read. No readable page, details limited to the tweet.
